title: Ten Things: 100 Practical Generative AI Prompts for In-House Lawyers
pub: Ten Things You Need to Know as In-House Counsel (tenthings.blog)
author: Sterling Miller

dom.t: Selective delegation: Rapid drafting proves little reliability

st.t: Selective delegation: Rapid drafting proves little reliability
st.an: Miller accepts selective, supervised delegation rather than lawyer replacement and materially develops the proposition with a practical operating model: treat AI as a junior assistant, provide context, iterate, verify uncertain outputs and use it chiefly for first drafts. He also adds concrete confidentiality and privacy safeguards, while offering experience-based guidance rather than systematic reliability or productivity evidence.
qs: Even though you must be prepared to check things for yourself, that does not diminish the value of what you do receive – certainly in terms of being a good first draft at a minimum.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the human-led augmentation model rather than wholesale lawyer replacement and concretely extends it with task-specific prompts for drafting, review, issue-spotting and summarisation, alongside confidentiality controls for in-house deployment. Its contribution is practical rather than evidentiary: it does not establish general competence, realised productivity or robust verification outcomes.
qs: If you take nothing else away from today’s post, consider this: Artificial intelligence will not replace lawyers, but lawyers who know how to use it properly will replace those who don’t.

To start, unless you have a bespoke Generative AI tool (i.e., one that is enterprise-level and/or tied only to the company’s own data), you need to be very careful what information you put into Generative AI.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source endorses the cluster’s core supervised-AI model: lawyers should use generative AI as a provisional drafting aid, supply context, iterate, and independently verify uncertain output. It also supports confidentiality controls, especially for non-bespoke tools. Although it argues that verification need not erase first-draft value and downplays lawyers’ need to understand technical mechanics, these are minor qualifications rather than rejection of the cluster’s proposition.
qs: Even though you must be prepared to check things for yourself, that does not diminish the value of what you do receive – certainly in terms of being a good first draft at a minimum.

kp.k: Executive pressure meets legal departments’ adoption constraints
kp.d: Drawing on questions received during 2024 and early 2025, Miller reports executive pressure for AI adoption and meaningful productivity gains. He attributes legal leaders’ caution to confidentiality, privilege, trustworthiness and prompt drafting, compounded by information overload and rapid technological change that most departments cannot resource a dedicated team to follow.
qs: There is a lot of pressure from the C-Suite on legal departments to adopt AI and show meaningful productivity gains.

Lastly, the technology is changing quickly, too quickly for most legal departments to understand the changes (and the implications) without a dedicated AI team – something beyond the reach (and budgets) of most in-house legal teams.

kp.k: Start with simple uses rather than sophisticated deployment
kp.d: Miller argues from personal experience that readily available, simple generative AI uses can improve in-house productivity without sophisticated adoption. His recommendation is incremental experimentation, starting with basic prompts and refining them toward more detailed, department-specific work; the article supplies practical examples rather than measured productivity results.
qs: In my experience, there are many simple and practical things you can do with Generative AI right now* that can drive real productivity gains for in-house lawyers.
The best way to learn what Generative AI can do is to start with simple prompts and then iterate and modify from there.

kp.k: Protect confidentiality and privilege before entering information
kp.d: Miller warns particularly about tools that are not bespoke enterprise-level systems or tied only to company data: inputs may be used for training, shared or breached. He recommends requests that avoid sensitive information and anonymisation where necessary, while stressing that replacing names takes time and does not remove other identifying or confidential material.
qs: Any information you put into the tool may be used to train it, may be shared with others, or may be the subject of a data breach.
Any one of these can put lawyers in a tough spot when it comes to protecting confidentiality and preventing waiver of
Don’t enter any information that is confidential or proprietary or that would reveal the names of clients or other information that could waive privilege.

kp.k: Privacy settings reduce but do not eliminate risks
kp.d: Using paid ChatGPT as his example, Miller recommends strong authentication, not supplying other account credentials, deleting conversations, temporary chats, clearing memory and disabling model-improvement sharing. He presents these controls as imperfect risk reduction, not a guarantee of confidentiality.
qs: Use the controls provided by the Generative AI tools to limit their ability to use your information.
Turn off “Improve model for everyone.”
None of this is perfect, but each will substantially reduce the risk of problems.

kp.k: Treat AI as supervised first-draft assistance
kp.d: Miller compares AI to an intern or summer associate requiring context, iterative supervision and human checking when the lawyer is unsure. His statement that hallucinations have been limited is explicitly personal experience, not a measured error rate. He argues that checking requirements do not negate first-draft value, framing AI as assistance rather than autonomous legal judgment.
qs: I personally have found that the number of times it simply makes stuff up (“hallucinates”) is limited.

I must (i) give it a lot of background and context for each assignment, (ii) follow up with them and iterate the work product, and (iii) if I am not sure about something, I will need to double check things myself.
Even though you must be prepared to check things for yourself, that does not diminish the value of what you do receive – certainly in terms of being a good first draft at a minimum.

kp.k: Prompt design shapes usefulness and business relevance
kp.d: Miller recommends specifying the task, output format, professional persona, audience, context and tone; requesting both sides’ arguments; breaking assignments into steps; and following up or modifying outputs. Examples translate legal analysis into business-friendly explanations and negotiation positions. These are practitioner recommendations, not comparative test findings.
qs: As you can imagine, the better the prompt, the better the results.
Write your explanations at a level an average business executive can understand.
As you can see, the more specifics and nuance you build into your prompt the more useful the results.

kp.k: Suggested applications span ten in-house practice areas
kp.d: The article provides 100 proposed prompts across commercial contracts, privacy and security, governance, employment, M&A, disputes, compliance, research, IP and technology, and department operations. Proposed tasks include drafting clauses and policies, identifying risks, explaining legal requirements, developing checklists and producing training materials. These are suggested uses, not documented deployments or validated outputs.
qs: I decided to set out 10 areas of the law and then under each set out 10 practical prompts you can use right now to get incredibly helpful and time-saving results from the Generative AI tool of your choice.
Review this contract (or clause) and identify risks related to indemnity, liability, termination, and exclusivity. Explain them in business-friendly language.
Create a 10-question multiple choice quiz to test employee understanding of anti-corruption and gifts & entertainment rules.

kp.k: AI can support legal operations and internal coordination
kp.d: Miller proposes using AI to draft intake forms, KPI dashboards, project trackers, executive updates, onboarding playbooks and guidance for junior lawyers and business teams. These examples extend the proposed productivity role beyond substantive legal drafting to department administration and communication with internal clients.
qs: Draft a standard legal ops KPI dashboard framework for tracking contract volume, turnaround time, litigation status, and legal spend.
Write a short guide for junior in-house lawyers on how to prioritize tasks and communicate effectively with business leaders.
Create a playbook outline for onboarding new in-house lawyers, including systems, team structure, and workflows.

kp.k: Detailed contract prompts organise review into staged workflows
kp.d: Miller’s advanced example sequences preliminary reading, clause-by-clause analysis, risk assessment, proposed revisions, legal and policy alignment, and a final report. It requests an executive summary, risk matrix, amendments and approval/revision/rejection recommendation. He argues that additional prompt preparation yields better results and suggests checking contracts against company playbooks or checklists.
qs: It takes a lot of work to create but you get back much better results:
Identify any material risks or ambiguities within the contract that could result in potential liability, disputes, or financial loss. Categorize these risks by severity (e.g., high, medium, low).
And if I have a contract playbook or checklist, I can ask the Generative AI to check the contract against that playbook or checklist.

kp.k: Build shared prompt libraries and practical prompting skills
kp.d: Miller recommends team-developed libraries of standard prompts tailored to company and department needs. He says useful prompting does not require computer-science expertise and asserts that mastery will increase a lawyer’s value by 10x; this is an unmeasured prospective claim, not an evidenced productivity multiplier.
qs: Fortunately, you do not need to be a computer scientist to prepare useful prompts as an in-house lawyer.
Those who do take the time to master it will increase their value to the department and the company by 10x.
One thing I highly recommend is for legal departments to work as a team to develop their own library of standard prompts tailored to the specific needs of the department and the company.

kp.k: AI competence will determine competitive replacement among lawyers
kp.d: Miller concludes with a prediction that lawyers using AI properly will replace those who do not, rather than AI directly replacing lawyers. This is a motivational competitive claim, with no stated timeframe or supporting labour-market evidence.
qs: Artificial intelligence will not replace lawyers, but lawyers who know how to use it properly will replace those who don’t.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Miller claims that simple generative AI uses can deliver immediate productivity gains for in-house lawyers without sophisticated deployment.
pts.d: He presents 100 prompts across contracts, privacy, governance, employment, transactions, disputes, compliance, research, IP, and legal department operations as practical ways to save time. Proposed uses include drafting, summarising, identifying risks, preparing checklists, and producing internal communications. These are proposed applications, not reported results from testing each prompt. The central framing is lawyer augmentation: useful initial work product with lawyer direction, iteration, and checking.

pts.k: Miller claims that more specific prompting improves usefulness and that developing prompting skills enables greater or more sophisticated output.
pts.d: He connects better results to specificity, context, persona, audience, format, stepwise instructions, follow-up, and iteration. His advanced contract-review example asks for clause analysis, risk assessment, revisions, policy alignment, and a final recommendation. He also proposes checking contracts against company playbooks and developing shared departmental prompt libraries. The multi-step prompt is an instruction example, not evidence of autonomous execution or reliable completion.

pts.k: Miller predicts a substantial professional advantage for lawyers who master AI, rather than replacement of lawyers by AI itself.
pts.d: He says mastering prompt drafting will increase a lawyer's value to the department and company by '10x' and concludes that AI-skilled lawyers will replace those who do not know how to use it properly. These are forward-looking professional-value and competitive-displacement claims, not quantified findings about productivity, wages, or employment.

pts.k: Miller describes executive pressure to adopt AI alongside confidentiality, privilege, reliability, and resource constraints that slow adoption.
pts.d: He reports that legal department leaders have reasons to proceed cautiously despite C-suite demands for productivity gains. Rapid technological change and information overload create adoption burdens, while dedicated AI teams are beyond most departments' budgets. He warns that information entered into tools may be used for training, shared, or exposed in a breach, and claims anonymisation and privacy controls reduce—but do not eliminate—risk.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies primarily on Miller's experience and practical illustrations, not measured productivity or labour-market evidence.
pts.d: Miller explicitly grounds immediate productivity benefits in his experience and describes the questions he received from in-house lawyers during 2024 and early 2025. His statement that hallucinations are limited is a personal observation, not a measured model error rate. The prompt examples illustrate suggested workflows but contain no outputs, controlled comparisons, timing measurements, or accuracy assessments. The article links to prompt-writing resources, prior articles, and privacy guides; these serve as practical references rather than presented empirical validation. No calculation or study is supplied for the '10x' value claim or the prediction that AI-skilled lawyers will replace others.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Productivity benefits are presented as available immediately as of 31 March 2025; professional displacement and longer-term prompt-library benefits have no specified deadline.
pts.d: The recommended adoption path starts with basic prompts and develops through experience and iteration. Usefulness depends on appropriate instructions and context, follow-up, and human verification where the lawyer is uncertain. Miller likens the tool to an intern or summer associate, rather than an independently reliable substitute. He stresses caution with confidential information, particularly outside bespoke enterprise-level or company-data tools, and acknowledges the time needed to sanitise documents. The five-year savings language in an example prompt requests an AI prediction about a contract management system; it is not Miller's own forecast of AI savings.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The primary affected group is corporate in-house legal teams, with benefits and risks extending to their companies and internal business clients.
pts.d: Individual in-house lawyers are expected to save time, produce more or more sophisticated work, and increase their professional value through AI competence. Legal department leaders face executive demands for gains while managing information risks and limited implementation resources. Companies and internal teams—including HR, sales, finance, executives, and project managers—are intended recipients of clearer explanations, training, policies, and more structured legal workflows. The closing replacement prediction refers to lawyers generally but offers no segment-specific employment forecast. The article does not predict law-firm staffing changes, ALSP market share, pricing changes, or access-to-justice outcomes.
